title: Truth alone wins
hook: India's motto comes from the Mundaka, and the full verse makes truth a road, not just a rule
carry: truth alone wins, and truth is the road
tomorrow: not by eye, not by speech

segments.voice: Yesterday: suparna, two birds on one tree. Your line was the one who watches is on your branch is on your branch.
screen: `THE ONE WHO WATCHES IS ON YOUR BRANCH IS ON YOUR BRANCH.`

segments.voice: If you've ever held Indian money, you've held this lesson. Look at the national emblem: the lions, back to back, taken from a pillar of the emperor Ashoka. Underneath them, in Devanagari script, three words. Satyameva jayate. Truth alone prevails. They're on Indian money, on government seals and documents. And they come from the Mundaka Upanishad, the chapter we're reading now. The full verse says a good deal more than the emblem has room for.
screen: `THE LIONS OF ASHOKA'S PILLAR.` → `SATYAMEVA JAYATE.` → `FROM THE MUNDAKA UPANISHAD.`

segments.voice: Here's Angiras's line: satyam eva jayate, nanritam. Truth alone wins, not untruth. Satya, truth, comes from sat, what is, what's real. So truth here is more than accurate words. It's being in line with what actually is. Eva means only, alone. And nanritam, not anritam: anrita is the crooked, the false, the opposite of rita, the right order of things. So: what is real wins. What's crooked doesn't. Then the verse keeps going, and this is the part the coins leave off. By truth the road is laid out, the path of the gods, on which the sages travel, their desires fulfilled, to the place where truth's highest treasure is. So truth isn't only the winner of an argument. It's a road. You walk on it, and it takes you somewhere. That fits the neighboring verses. Just before this, the Mundaka says the self is reached by truth, by austerity, by right knowledge, by the steady life of a student. Truthfulness isn't a rule stuck on the outside of spiritual life. It's the pavement. That's why Hindu teaching counts satya as part of dharma for everyone, and the Yoga Sutra lists it among the first restraints, the yamas, right after not harming. The words became the motto beneath the national emblem when India became a republic, in 1950. It doesn't claim that truth wins quickly, or every day, or in every courtroom. The Upanishad's claim is longer and quieter: over the whole road, what is real holds, and what's crooked doesn't. Which means the small fib counts too. Not as a crime: as one crooked stone in your own road.
screen: `TRUTH ALONE WINS, NOT UNTRUTH.` · `SATYA: WHAT IS REAL.` · `BY TRUTH THE ROAD IS LAID.` · `SATYA IS PART OF DHARMA.` · then, large: `SATYAMEVA JAYATE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small place in your life where something is a little crooked: a fib told to keep the peace, a thing you said you'd do and didn't, a story you tell yourself that isn't quite so. No shame; just look at it plainly. Then picture what it would be like to set that one stone straight, and rest in that picture.
Satya, truth, what is real. Satyam eva jayate, from Mundaka 3.1: truth alone wins, not untruth, and by truth the road of the gods is laid.
Your line: truth alone wins, and truth is the road. Tomorrow, how the self is seen, and how it isn't. Day four hundred eighteen, done.

Ashoka.meaning: an emperor of ancient India; his lion pillar became the emblem

Devanagari.meaning: the script used to write Sanskrit and Hindi

Mundaka.meaning: an Upanishad of the Atharva Veda

Angiras.meaning: the sage whose teaching to Shaunaka is the Mundaka

yamas.meaning: the restraints that begin the yoga path: not harming, truthfulness and more

dharma.meaning: right living, duty, the order that holds life together

sources.ref: Mundaka Upanishad 3.1.5 (the self reached by truth, discipline, right knowledge)

Yoga Sutra 2.30 (the yamas: ahimsa, satya, asteya, brahmacharya, aparigraha)

notes: Verse numbering: satyam eva jayate is 3.1.6 in most editions. Confirm.

Emblem facts: adopted 26 January 1950, motto in Devanagari beneath the Lion Capital of Ashoka at Sarnath. Confirm, and confirm the motto appears on Indian coins as well as banknotes (the carry, fixed by the index, says 'coins'; some coin series show the emblem without the motto).
Malaviya popularizing the phrase is commonly stated (e.g. at the 1918 Congress session); hedged as 'many people credit'. Confirm or cut.
Etymology: satya from sat; anrta as the negation of rta. Standard; confirm.
Some manuscripts/readings give jayati for jayate; not raised in the script.
